Introduction - September 2011 











#### **Sentiment turns bearish as LME Week approaches** 

With the metals industry gathering in London for LME Week in early October, it is an ideal time to review the events of the last twelve months and, more importantly, assess the prospects for 2012.  Thomson Reuters GFMS have extended our supply-demand and balance forecasts out to 2012 on both an annual and quarterly basis.  We have also reviewed our projectio

ns for the rest of 2011. 

Despite the heightened volatility over the last year, prices are relatively close to levels seen one year ago.  The comparison of the difference between the high and the low however tells a different story, and provides a more accurate view of the base metals performance over the last twelve months.  Prices of all the base metals are well below recent peaks (double digit declines in all cases).  The falls range from around 12% for copper to above 25% for nickel and tin. 

##### **What a difference a year makes** 

LME Week often proves to be a turning point in the base metals market as a broad consensus can emerge.  Our discussions with traders, producers and consumers point to a more cautious price outlook this year.  A number of drivers that supported the market have begun to fade, or possibly have gone into reverse.  The rapid rebound in demand in the mature economies supported by restocking and earlier stimulus packages and the various industryspecific measures has come to an end.  We are seeing little or no growth from this source.  This trend was becoming increasingly apparent even before a worsening of the debt crisis within the EU.  Also the specific measures to assist the auto sector have come to an end. 

an end and we are looking for a return of strong apparent consumption growth in 2012 from China.  Fixed asset investment is still growing at around 25%, while although industrial output has slowed slightly it remains comfortably in double figures of 13.5% in July.  Although we note the slowdown in the auto sector, other important base metal consuming sectors such as refrigerators, air-conditioners and consumer electronics are still registering strong growth.  As such, we expect that Chinese imports of refined base metals will pick up in the latter part of this year and will be carried over to 2012. 

##### **Other BRIC nations and ASEAN countries will support demand growth** 

Although China has dominated the demand environment, one should not ignore the contribution of the other BRICs, which typically account for between 6-10% of global demand.  Elsewhere, 2010 saw a sharp rebound in South Korea and to a less extent Taiwan.  Although we expect that consumption growth has suffered due to a dip in exports to the EU and North America, we note that intra-Asian trade is holding up well.  A similar pattern is emerging from within the ASEAN countries.  Domestic demand remains positive although there are some concerns about export levels to the mature economies.  Although Thomson Reuters GFMS have taken a relatively positive view that there will not be a double-dip recession when preparing our forecast for the remainder of this year and for 2012, the downside risk is obviously increasing.  We will be tracking the more forwardlooking indicators closely in the coming months. 

##### **Supply:  Growth is not that threatening** 

On the supply side, given current prices there is no incentive for producers to cut back de

Economic Indicators - September 2011 











The indicators relating to the manufacturing sector in the United States are also pointing lower.  The closely-watched ISM index fell for the sixth month in a row to 50.9, now perilously close to the 50 threshold between economic expansion and contraction.  Of particular concern is the decline in new orders, which now stand below the key 50 level. 

The Eurozone economic sentiment index declined in August to its lowest level in more than a year, slipping back below 100 to 98.3.  All the key metal consuming sectors – manufacturing, construction and consumer – registered declines. Sovereign debt and high unemployment levels are the main triggers for the weak outlook.  Neither of these two “negatives” are likely to be resolved in the near future. 

China’s fixed asset investment maintained its strong 

growth, advancing by 25% in August.  This series has been remarkably stable with it remaining

above 25 since February, when it dipped to 24.9. The only major sector to exhibit some slight weakness was transport with both autos and rail transport showing easing growth rates. In the auto sector, this primarily reflects a tightening of standards concerning fuel-efficient vehicles, which has adversely affected output growth. A series of railway accidents has put some expansion plans on hold in this sector. Japan’s consumer confidence index slipped to 37.4 in August from 37.7 in July. The spectre of deflation still hangs over the Japanese market. In addition, the strengthening of the yen may hit exports, which may partially offset the boost from post-earthquake reconstruction. The quarterly Tankan survey has moved back into positive territory, albeit from an exceptionally low base. Expansion in India is easing slightly in response to the government’s attempts to curb inflationary pressures. Real GDP growth slipped to 7.7% in the second quarter, down from 8.8% a year earlier. However, positive underlying fundamentals remain in place. Rising employment and consumer expenditure should support copper demand growth. developments** 

- **_As noted in our earlier research, aluminium prices staged a sharp correction earlier in the summer that saw them fall by 12.0% to around $2,450/tonne in mid-July.  Since then, there has been further weakness with cash prices slipping below $2,400/tonne._** 

- **_Aluminium continues to be faced with a large LME stockpile that is overhanging the market. As the bulk of this is tied up in long-term bank financing deals, only a fraction of total LME stocks are available to the market.  The lack of physical availability has in turn seen physical premiums remain high.  However, if interest rates rise as governments try to curb inflationary pressures, some of the warehousing deals could begin to unwind._** 

- **_Chinese imports of primary aluminium fell by 25% year-on-year to 147,000 tonnes over the first seven months of the year, reflecting a combination of a narrow arbitrage between prices on the LME and SHFE and record high domestic production._** 

- **_We are beginning to see a slowdown in the rate of production growth in China and in the mature economies. The process of the reactivation of idled capacity in the mature economies and China is coming to an end.  The latest data from the International  Aluminium Institute suggest that production up to July increased by 5.8%._** 

##### **Outlook for the next 12 months** 

- **_Thomson Reuters GFMS are continuing to project the aluminium market in a sizeable surplus of 459,000 tonnes in 2011, as rising output in China up to August helps global output to record growth of 5.4%, following a 10.3% increase last year.  The increase to production will be partially offset nevertheless by challenged by strong demand growth of 6.2%._** 

- **_The aluminium price had previously received support from a shift in the cost curve due to high energy prices.  However, with the metal’s weak fundamentals and concerns over the health of the global economy, we expect prices to continue trending lower.  This should see the spot price average $2,476/tonne over the fourth quarter, which gives an average for the year of $2,500/tonne._** 

- **_Under Scenario B, we expect improving demand coupled with falling Chinese output to see prices average $2,664/tonne in 2011.  Under Scenario C, we simply expect the reverse. This should see the aluminium price average $2,300/tonne this year._**

As such, we expect stainless steel surcharges to fall in October, which in turn will leave stainless service centers with high-priced inventory. Consequently, not only will this discourage consumers from buying, but will also reduce distributors’ purchases from mills as well as the mills’ raw material requirements. The spot market has also been fairly quiet, with no buyers taking advantage of lower prices to get extra material due to the macroeconomic turmoil. This has kept melting-grade premiums steady at between 30-50 cents/lb, while premiu

ms for plating-grade material are still between 65-90 cents/lb. China’s largest stainless producers, Taigang Stainless, conducted a week-long maintenance in August on one its hot-rolling plants to support prices amid a weak domestic stainless market. Based on the capacity of the plant, the maintenance work may reduce production by 40,000-50,000 tonnes. Taigang produced 1.46 million tonnes of stainless steel in the first half of 2011, up just 3.5% on the same period a year ago. There have been reports that Ningbo Baoxin also plans to do maintenance work this month. ##### **China is also the main driver on the demand-side** Estimates by the WBMS suggest that global nickel consumption continued to trend higher year-on-year on a cumulative basis, despite easing growth in stainless steel production over the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, China was the main contributor to the growth helped in part by the 10% cumulative growth in imports of refined metal. This is further supported by statistics by the Stainless Steel Council of China (CSSC), which estimate that China produced 6.21 million tonnes of crude stainless steel over the first half, up by 13.5% year-on-year, of which chrome-nickel (300-series) output was up almost 30% year-on-year at 3.62 million tonnes. Interestingly, demand excluding China grew by a mere 1.5% year-on-year. The latest trade statistics by the CNI-A show that Chinese net imports of refined nickel increased to their highest level in almost two-years in July. At 16,483 tonnes, they were up 37.4% on the previous month and 65% higher than the lowest net-import figure this year of 9,988 tonnes recorded in February. ##### **Downtrend in Chinese supply seen over July** 

The most recent data released by the CNIA shows that Chinese refined tin production declined by 8.3% monthon-month in July to 12,096 tonnes.  Although the total still represented a 6.9% year-on-year increase, this was the third consecutive month-on-month fall seen since April.  Moreover, Chinese mine output also showed a similar trend, with 7,087 tonnes of tin-in-concentrate being produced over July, up 28.2% year-on-year but down 14.7% month-on-month. Over the aforementioned period, some miners and smelters in China cut or suspended production, largely as a result of power supply restrictions and environmental regulations, in addition to slack demand over the summer months. 

##### **Latin American problems add to raw material tightness** 

Thomson Reuters GFMS expect global mine production growth to total just 2.3% this year, after experiencing three years of negative growth.  This has been downwardly revised from our previous forecast in light of the underperformance within Latin America.  Most prominently, Peruvian mine production has declined by 13.4% over the year-to-date. Elsewhere in the region, the start up of Silver Standard Resources’ Pirquitas mine in Argentina continues to be delayed, and the company has given no indication of production volumes or scheduled start dates at the 2,500 

tonne per year operation.  We expect that this will also serve to restrict the growth in the region’s refined production over the year, as discussed in the market outlook section.

Following a softening of demand over the traditionally weak summer months, including in key consumer China, we expect tin demand to pick up over the close of the current quarter and over the fourth quarter of the year.
